newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir crew face long wait to finish repairs.
newsitem.headline: Mir crew face long wait to finish repairs.

text.p: The Russian-American crew of the damaged Mir space station must wait nearly two weeks for supplies before completing power supply repairs but have as yet no plans to evacuate, a Russian official said on Thursday.

"The cosmonauts will have to make a space walk to complete the repairs to the Spektr module. For that, special equipment should be delivered to the Mir station on the Progress cargo craft," Russian Space Agency chief Yuri Koptev told reporters.
He said the freighter would not be launched for 11 days.

The unmanned Progress cargo craft had been due to leave on a routine supply mission on Friday. Koptev said it had now been postponed by 10 days to gather equipment needed for repairs. The trip from Baikonur launch pad to Mir typically takes two days.
"At present there is no danger for the cosmonauts. They feel fine, although they went through a bit of stress yesterday," said Koptev, the agency's general director.

"There are no grounds for evacuating the cosmonauts from Mir at the moment...An evacuation could take place if the air pressure in the main module fell below 550 mm of mercury (just under three quarters of normal atmospheric pressure)," he told reporters at the Mission Control centre near Moscow.
The Spektr module was holed by a docking probe from another unmanned Progress craft during manoeuvres on Wednesday in the ageing Mir station's worst accident of recent years.
Film showed a smooth round hole several centimetres (inches) wide in the wall of the Spektr module, which was sealed off along with considerable quantities of equipment.
The collision also damaged a solar panel, prompting loss of electricity from the module, which normally supplies 55 percent of Mir's power.

A meeting of a 72-strong expert committee, which includes Mir's chief designer and representatives of the U.S. space agency NASA, began at 0930 GMT at Korolyov. Officials said the meeting was likely to go on until 1800 GMT.
Koptev said the air pressure in the main module had been restored after an initial drop.
But a repositioning of Mir to correct a misalignment of its solar panels after the collision had not fully corrected the problem. The lack of power meant the crew was sending no television pictures.
